'''Nima Arkani-Hamed''' ({{langx|fa|نیما ارکانی حامد}}; born April 5, 1972) is an Iranian-American-Canadian<ref name="sns.ias.edu">[https://web.archive.org/web/20160419001406/http://www.sns.ias.edu/ckfinder/userfiles/files/4-17-15NAH_CV-Biblio.pdf "Curriculum Vita, updated 4-17-15"], sns.ias.edu; accessed December 4, 2015.</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-01-01|title=Nima Arkani-Hamed|url=https://ir.usembassy.gov/nima-arkani-hamed/|access-date=2020-07-17|website=U.S. Virtual Embassy Iran|language=en-US}}</ref> [[theoretical physics|theoretical]] [[physicist]], with interests in [[high-energy physics]], [[quantum field theory]], [[string theory]], [[physical cosmology|cosmology]] and [[accelerator physics|collider physics]]. Arkani-Hamed is a member of the permanent faculty at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/arkani-hamed|title=Nima Arkani-Hamed|website=Institute for Advanced Study|language=en|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref> where he is also director of the Carl P. Feinberg Cross-Disciplinary Program in Innovation. He is also director of The Center for Future High Energy Physics (CFHEP) in [[Beijing]], China.<ref>{{Cite web|title = CFHEP|url = http://cfhep.ihep.ac.cn/|website = cfhep.ihep.ac.cn|access-date = 2016-02-09}}</ref>

==Early life==
Nima Arkani-Hamed was born on April 5, 1972, in [[Houston]], [[Texas]], to Jafargholi "Jafar" Arkani-Hamed and Hamideh Alasti, both [[physicist]]s from [[Iran]].<ref name="mit">Jafargholi "Jafar" Arkani-Hamed. [http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/58240/29576858.pdf?sequence1 Lateral Variations of Density in the Earth's Mantle]. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130926101314/http://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/58240/29576858.pdf?sequence1 |date=September 26, 2013 }}</ref> His father, a native of [[Tabriz]],<ref>Cornellcast: [https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/handle/1721.1/58240/29576858-MIT.pdf?sequence=2].</ref> worked for the [[Apollo program|NASA Apollo program]] in the 1970s,<ref name="Wired">{{cite news|last1=Wolchover|first1=Natalie|title=Visions of Future Physics|url=https://www.wired.com/2015/10/visions-future-physics/|access-date=11 July 2018|work=[[Wired (website)|Wired]]|date=4 October 2015}}</ref> and later taught [[earth science|earth]] and [[planetary science]]s at [[McGill University]] in [[Montreal]].<ref name=PBS>{{cite web|title=Professor Nima Arkani-Hamed Wins Prestigious Physics Prize|url=https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/pages/frontline/tehranbureau/2012/08/news-professor-nima-arkani-hamed-wins-prestigious-physics-prize.html#ixzz251JTtZqj|publisher=Public Broadcasting Service|access-date=August 30, 2012}}</ref> 

Arkani-Hamed spent his early childhood in the United States.<ref name="Wolchover">{{cite news|last1=Wolchover|first1=Natalie|title=Visions of Future Physics|url=https://www.wired.com/2015/10/visions-future-physics/|access-date=5 October 2015|work=[[Wired (website)|Wired]]|date=4 October 2015}}</ref> In 1979, following the [[Iranian Revolution]], he and his family returned to Iran after the new government claimed that greater freedom of expression and new opportunities would be available.<ref name="Wolchover"/> However, the start of the [[Cultural Revolution in Iran|Islamic Cultural Revolution]] in 1980 led to the forceful closures of universities across Iran.<ref name="Wolchover"/> Arkani-Hamed's father, Jafar, who at the time was chairman of the physics department at [[Sharif University of Technology]] in [[Tehran]], wrote a petition with faculty, denouncing the closures.<ref name="Wolchover"/> Arkani-Hamed's father and his colleagues were subsequently marked for arrest by the Islamic regime officials.<ref name="Wolchover"/> As a result, the family went underground and spent their life savings to flee to [[Canada]].<ref name="Wolchover"/>

==Academic career==
Arkani-Hamed graduated from the [[University of Toronto]] with a [[Joint honours degree|joint honours]] degree in [[mathematics]] and [[physics]] in 1993. He then pursued graduate studies at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he worked under the supervision of [[Lawrence John Hall|Lawrence Hall]]. Most of Arkani-Hamed's graduate work focused on [[supersymmetry]] and [[flavor (physics)|flavor physics]]; his doctoral dissertation, titled ''Supersymmetry and Hierarchies'', was completed in 1997. He subsequently conducted postdoctoral research in the [[SLAC Theory Group]] at [[Stanford University]], where he collaborated with [[Savas Dimopoulos]] and [[Giorgi Dvali]]  on the development of the paradigm of [[large extra dimensions]].<ref name="Wired"/>

In 1999, Arkani-Hamed joined the faculty of the University of California, Berkeley Department of Physics. In January 2001, he took a leave of absence from Berkeley to visit [[Harvard University]] and later remained there as a professor from 2002 to 2008.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Physics Tree - Nima Arkani-Hamed|url=https://academictree.org/physics/peopleinfo.php?pid=169937|access-date=2021-03-07|website=academictree.org}}</ref> In 2008, he joined the School of Natural Sciences at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey|Princeton]], [[New Jersey]], as a professor, and in 2021 he became the inaugural Carl P. Feinberg Director of the Cross-Disciplinary Program there.<ref>[https://www.ias.edu/news/2021/cpf-cross-disciplinary-program-in-innovation-established Carl P. Feinberg Cross-Disciplinary Program in Innovation Established at IAS], IAS.edu; accessed May 7, 2021.</ref><ref>[https://www.ias.edu/press-releases/theoretical-physicist-nima-arkani-hamed-appointed-faculty-institute-advanced-study Theoretical Physicist Nima Arkani-Hamed Appointed to the Faculty of the Institute for Advanced Study], ias.edu; accessed May 12, 2015.</ref>

Since 2013, Arkani-Hamed has been a leading figure in research on the [[amplituhedron]], a geometric structure that simplifies calculations of [[particle]] interactions in certain [[quantum field]] theories.

==Honors and awards==

In 2003, Arkani-Hamed won the [[Gribov Medal]] of the [[European Physical Society]], and in the summer of 2005 while at Harvard he won the [[Phi Beta Kappa]] chapter's award for teaching excellence. In 2008, he won the Raymond and Beverly Sackler Prize given at [[Tel Aviv University]] to young scientists who have made outstanding and fundamental contributions in Physical Science.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://english.tau.ac.il/sackler_prize_in_physics_past_laureates |title=Past Laureates of the Raymond and Beverly Sackler International Prize in Physics |access-date=November 12, 2017 |archive-date=October 16, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171016014757/https://english.tau.ac.il/sackler_prize_in_physics_past_laureates |url-status=dead }}</ref> He was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2009.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780-2010: Chapter A|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterA.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=April 25, 2011}}</ref> He gave the [[Messenger lectures]] at Cornell University in 2010, and  was an 
[[Andrew Dickson White|A. D. White]] Professor-at-Large at [[Cornell University]] from 2013 to 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://adwhiteprofessors.cornell.edu/professors-at-large/|title=Andrew D. White Professors-at-Large|language=en|access-date=2019-02-19}}</ref> In 2012 he was an inaugural awardee of the [[Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics]], the creation of physicist and internet entrepreneur, [[Yuri Milner]].<ref>[https://breakthroughprize.org/News/15 New annual US$3 million Fundamental Physics Prize recognizes transformative advances in the field] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120803211628/https://breakthroughprize.org/News/15 |date=2012-08-03 }}.</ref> He was one of six physicists featured in the award-winning 2013 documentary film ''[[Particle Fever]]'', and was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2017. In 2021, he was awarded the [[Sakurai Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]].

== Personal views ==
Nima  identifies himself as an [[Atheism|atheist]]. On 21 April 2016, he gave a public talk titled, ''The Morality of Fundamental Physics'' at Cornell University and said:<blockquote>...part of my motivation for giving this talk is that like many physicists, many scientists, I'm an atheist. But unlike some atheists, I'm certainly not a militant atheist. And I dislike a lot a certain strand of militant atheism.... I don't believe in God. I do, however, think that instead of worshiping a vast and unknowable God, we can devote ourselves to this slow unveiling of the vastness of truth in all of its glory....<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nima Arkani-Hamed: The Morality of Fundamental Physics |url=https://vod.video.cornell.edu/media/1_esceq1wg |access-date=2025-01-04 |website=Cornell Video |language=en}}</ref></blockquote>
